Aghast

/uh-GAST/ — rhymes with vast · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Someone who is aghast is struck with sudden shock, horror, or disbelief at what they see or hear.

The audience sat aghast as the magician appeared to saw the box in half.

Worked Example

A museum curator discovers that a famous painting on display is actually a worthless forgery, and her face goes pale as she stands aghast before the frame.

The curator's sudden shock and disbelief at the deception is exactly what aghast captures. 'Shocked' could work, but aghast adds that extra layer of horror—the realization strikes her all at once, and she's overcome by the dismay of it all.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

shocked: suddenly upset by something completely unexpected

horrified: filled with dread at something terrible

startled: briefly surprised by something sudden

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

composed: calm and steady when others are shocked

unfazed: not surprised or bothered at all

Where it sits · how completely the sight stuns you — startled → shocked → horrified → aghast

startled vs. aghast: Startled is much weaker than aghast: a startled person jumps at a sudden noise and recovers instantly, while someone aghast is frozen in open-mouthed horror.

shocked vs. aghast: Shocked is weaker than aghast; shock is the jolt of the unexpected, but aghast adds horror and disbelief so strong the person can barely respond.

horrified vs. aghast: Horrified is nearly as strong as aghast, but aghast pushes one step further — it captures the visible, stunned moment when horror leaves you speechless and staring.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — a-

Prefix — a-: thoroughly, completely (intensive) (Old English)

Root — ghast

Root — ghast: to terrify (from a word for spirit, ghost) (Old English)

Put it together

Put it together: Aghast joins the old intensive prefix a-, 'thoroughly,' with the root ghast, from Old English gaestan, 'to terrify' — a relative of ghost and ghastly. It literally means 'thoroughly terrified,' as if you had just seen a ghost; the gh spelling was even added later by association with ghost.

Use the root in a new word: ghastly

Use the root in a new word: ghastly: The movie's ghastly final scene was so horrifying that the whole audience sat aghast — both words grow from the same Old English root for terror.

Word Choice

formal / literary

Aghast paints a picture of sudden, overwhelming shock mixed with horror or disbelief. Use it when the moment hits hard and visibly. For mild surprise, 'shocked' does the job; for everyday disappointment, reach for 'disappointed' instead.
